word:greek-nt:G0024.explanation: Aganaktēsis means indignation, a feeling of anger or vexation.

word:greek-nt:G0099.explanation: This word refers to the Adriatic Sea, a specific body of water named in the Greek New Testament. It functions as a geographic name rather than a description of a person, action, or quality. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 27:27. Its basic meaning is therefore straightforward: the Adriatic Sea. The surrounding passage is needed to explain what was happening there, but the name itself identifies the sea.

word:greek-nt:G0226.explanation: This Greek word means “be truthful” or “to be truthful.” It expresses the act of speaking or behaving in a truthful way rather than falsely. As a verb, it describes what someone does: living or communicating in keeping with what is true. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, appearing once in Galatians and once in Ephesians. Its precise emphasis in either verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage.

word:greek-nt:G0312.explanation: Anangellō means to report, tell, or announce information. It can describe telling others what happened, as when a man told the Jews who had made him well.

word:greek-nt:G0420.explanation: This word describes someone who is not resentful—one who does not keep bitterness or hostility toward others. It points to an attitude free from stored grievance rather than merely a temporary absence of anger. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, so its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. Its central meaning remains clear: not resentful.

word:greek-nt:G0482.explanation: Antilambanō means to help or take hold of something. It can also describe sharing in a benefit.

word:greek-nt:G0569.explanation: Apisteō means to disbelieve or refuse belief.

word:greek-nt:G0608.explanation: Apokleio means to shut or close.

word:greek-nt:G0671.explanation: This word means “using up.” It describes the action of using something until its available use is exhausted. It functions as a verb, focusing on what happens to something through use rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Colossians 2:22. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is the completion or exhaustion of something through being used.

word:greek-nt:G0745.explanation: Archelaus is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Matthew 2:22, and is rendered as “Archelaus.” Because it is a proper name, its basic meaning is the person it identifies; the surrounding passage is needed to explain that person’s role in the verse. The name itself does not function as a common noun or verb.

word:greek-nt:G0806.explanation: Asphalōs means safely or securely, and it can also mean certainly.

word:greek-nt:G0891.explanation: This word means “until” and marks the point up to which an action, condition, or period continues. It sets a time boundary: something remains true or keeps happening before that stated point, and the wording directs attention to what happens when the limit is reached. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 49 times, showing regular use for expressing temporal limits. Its basic sense remains the same whether the boundary concerns an event, a period, or another stated time.

word:greek-nt:G0943.explanation: Batos means a bath, a liquid measure. It can also refer to a bush.

word:greek-nt:G1009.explanation: Botrys means a cluster or bunch of grapes.

word:greek-nt:G1100.explanation: Glōssa means the tongue. It can also mean a language. A nation may be distinguished by its tongue.

word:greek-nt:G1247.explanation: Diakoneō means to serve, including waiting at table.

word:greek-nt:G1290.explanation: Diaspora means dispersion or scattering abroad. In Scripture, it can refer to Jewish people scattered among the nations.

word:greek-nt:G1315.explanation: This Greek New Testament word means “to kill,” describing the act of causing someone’s death. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, both times in Acts. Its basic meaning remains direct and concrete: someone is put to death. The surrounding passage determines who performs the action and why, but the word itself identifies the deadly act without adding a separate motive or spiritual interpretation.

word:greek-nt:G1456.explanation: Enkainia means dedication and can refer to the Feast of Dedication.

word:greek-nt:G1504.explanation: Eikōn means an image or likeness.

word:greek-nt:G1650.explanation: This Greek New Testament word refers to “certainty” or “rebuke.” It can name something that gives firm confidence, or a corrective response that confronts wrong. The two glosses point to a settled assurance on one side and a forceful correction on the other; the surrounding wording determines which sense is active. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Hebrews 11:1.

word:greek-nt:G1687.explanation: Embateuō means to enter, set foot on, or intrude into something. It describes intruding into things not seen.

word:greek-nt:G1773.explanation: This word describes something happening at night, especially while it is still dark before daylight. It functions as a time expression, telling when an action occurs rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, at Mark 1:35. Its basic sense is therefore a nighttime setting; the surrounding verse determines the particular action being described. The two stated meanings emphasize both the nighttime period and the darkness that remains.

word:greek-nt:G1852.explanation: Exypnizo means to wake out of sleep.

word:greek-nt:G1993.explanation: This word means “to silence”—to stop someone from speaking or prevent speech from continuing. It describes an action directed toward a speaker, rather than merely becoming quiet oneself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Titus 1:11, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea remains clear: bringing speech to an end or rendering a person unable to continue speaking.

word:greek-nt:G2031.explanation: This word means “a word” or “word.” It refers to a verbal expression—a unit of speech used to communicate something. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, in Hebrews 7:9. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise force in that sentence must be understood from its context. Its basic sense remains a spoken or written word rather than an action, person, or place.

word:greek-nt:G2048.explanation: Eremos describes something deserted or desolate. It can also refer to a desert place.

word:greek-nt:G2185.explanation: This Greek New Testament word means “to come” or “to reach.” It describes arriving at a place, person, or intended point. In its two New Testament occurrences, it is rendered “reach,” including the idea of reaching people or territory within the proper scope of one’s work. The word functions as an action: someone comes to or reaches what lies ahead. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains movement toward an intended destination or boundary.

word:greek-nt:G2260.explanation: “Than” is a comparison word. It connects two people, things, or choices and indicates that one is being preferred, valued, or regarded above the other. Its meaning is relational: it does not describe an object by itself, but helps express a comparison between alternatives. This Greek New Testament word occurs once, in John 12:43. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic function remains to mark comparison.

word:greek-nt:G2394.explanation: Iason is the personal name Jason.

word:greek-nt:G2479.explanation: Ischus means strength, power, might, force, or ability. It describes the strength devoted fully to loving God. It also describes ability supplied for service.

word:greek-nt:G2516.explanation: Kathezomai means to sit, sit down, or be seated. It describes the act of sitting, as when Jesus sat down by a well.

word:greek-nt:G2602.explanation: Katabolē means a foundation. It can also describe a beginning, as in the foundation of the world. In another use, it refers to conception, as Sarah received strength to conceive.

word:greek-nt:G2677.explanation: Katartismos means perfecting: bringing something into a condition of fitness and readiness.

word:greek-nt:G2754.explanation: Kenodoxia means vainglory or empty pride.

word:greek-nt:G2840.explanation: Koinoō means to make unclean or pollute. It can also describe treating something as unclean.

word:greek-nt:G2897.explanation: Kraipalē means drunken dissipation, or surfeiting.

word:greek-nt:G2938.explanation: Ktisma means a created thing or creature.

word:greek-nt:G3036.explanation: Lithoboleō means to stone or throw stones at someone.

word:greek-nt:G3418.explanation: Mnēma means a tomb, a place where someone is laid.

word:greek-nt:G3461.explanation: Myrias means a myriad, a group of ten thousand.

word:greek-nt:G3663.explanation: Homoiopathēs means having like feelings and passions, as others do.

word:greek-nt:G3766.explanation: Oukoun means therefore or so then.

word:greek-nt:G3788.explanation: Ophthalmos means eye, the physical organ of sight. It can also refer figuratively to the mind’s eye, as when opened eyes are linked with recognition.

word:greek-nt:G3814.explanation: Paidiskē means a female servant or maidservant. It can also refer to a young girl.

word:greek-nt:G3937.explanation: Parmenas is the name of one of the seven deacons chosen at Jerusalem.

word:greek-nt:G3942.explanation: Paroimia means a proverb. It can also describe figurative speech that conveys meaning through figures rather than plain words.

word:greek-nt:G4064.explanation: Periphero means to carry around. It can also describe being driven to and fro.

word:greek-nt:G4118.explanation: Pleistos means the greatest or very great. It can also mean the most, as when most of the mighty works had been done in certain cities.

word:greek-nt:G4161.explanation: This word means “what is made” or “workmanship”: something produced by a maker. It points to the result of making rather than to the act itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Romans 1:20 and Ephesians 2:10. Thus, it is a word about something made or produced. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the work or result brought forth by a maker.

word:greek-nt:G4266.explanation: Proginomai means to happen previously—to come about beforehand.

word:greek-nt:G4288.explanation: Prothumia means readiness. It can also describe willingness.

word:greek-nt:G4363.explanation: Prospiptō means to fall down before someone. In another sense, it describes wind beating against a house.

word:greek-nt:G4419.explanation: Pterygion means a highest point, or pinnacle.

word:greek-nt:G4536.explanation: Salpinx means a trumpet. It can also refer to the sound made by a trumpet.

word:greek-nt:G4730.explanation: Stenochōria means great distress or anguish.

word:greek-nt:G4792.explanation: Synkomizō means to bear away together, as in carrying away a corpse, and can also mean to bury or entomb.

word:greek-nt:G4833.explanation: Συμμορφιζόμενος means to be conformed or brought into the same form.

word:greek-nt:G4910.explanation: Syneuōcheomai means to feast sumptuously with others.

word:greek-nt:G5117.explanation: Topos means a place or region. It can also refer to a seat or position, as when someone takes the lowest place at a table.

word:greek-nt:G5162.explanation: Trophos means a nurse or nursing mother.

word:greek-nt:G5243.explanation: This word means “arrogance” or “pride”—an attitude of thinking too highly of oneself and elevating oneself above others. It describes a self-exalting inward posture rather than ordinary confidence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Mark 7:22. Its listed English rendering is “pride,” which closely expresses the central idea. The precise force of the word in that occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

word:greek-nt:G5306.explanation: Hysteros means later or afterward, and can also mean the latter or last in a sequence.

word:greek-nt:G5470.explanation: Chalkous means made of bronze or brass.

word:greek-nt:G5513.explanation: This word means “lukewarm,” describing something that is only mildly warm rather than hot. It is an adjective used to characterize a condition or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Revelation 3:16. Its basic meaning is straightforward: it identifies something lacking full heat, intensity, or warmth. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself refers to a tepid or lukewarm state.

word:greek-nt:G6022.explanation: This word means “to slander” or “to be slandered”: it concerns speaking falsely or harmfully against someone, or being treated that way. As a verb, it can describe either the act of attacking another person’s reputation or the experience of receiving such accusations. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 4:13, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

word:greek-nt:G6080.explanation: This word means a “relative,” referring to a person connected to someone through family ties. It is used as a noun to identify a family connection rather than an action, quality, or object. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Luke 1:36. Its precise reference in that verse must be understood from the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning remains a family relation.
